newsitem.title: UK: First bomb since IRA truce blown up in N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: First bomb since IRA truce blown up in N.Ireland.

text.p: The British army carried out a controlled explosion on Friday on the first bomb found since the Irish Republican Army (IRA) called a truce in its war against British rule in Northern Ireland 11 days ago.
The device, believed to contain up to 1,000 lbs (450 kg) of home-made explosive, was thought to have been planted near a lakeside holiday complex by a breakaway republican group.
Boats and hotels were evacuated around the hotel at Lisbellaw in County Fermanagh, about 100 miles (160 km) west of Belfast. There were no injuries.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the bomb. Police said they were alerted to the device by two telephone calls but gave no further details.
The incident was similar to one in the same area 14 months ago during Protestant-Catholic sectarian upheaval in Northern Ireland, when a bomb rocked another tourist hotel, injuring several people.
It underlined that, while Northern Ireland's key pro-British Protestant and Catholic republican guerrilla groups have declared ceasefires, a host of breakaway organisations have not.

The Continuity Army Council (CAC), responsible for the hotel bomb last year, is linked to Republican Sinn Fein, an organisation which itself broke away from Sinn Fein, political wing of the IRA, in the 1970s in a policy row.
It is opposed to negotiations with Britain and says that an end to rule of Northern Ireland by London will only come about by force of arms.

Its extremist "no talks" philosophy is shared by the Irish National Liberation Army (INLA), an IRA splinter group which shot at police patrols during rioting in Belfast last month over Protestant Orange Order parades, seen as inflammatory by Catholics.

The attempted bombing came 24 hours after a maverick pro-British "loyalist" group, which accuses the Republic of Ireland government of seeking to take over Northern Ireland, said it was on the warpath.
The Loyalist Volunteer Force (LVF) broke away from the main loyalist factions after they called a ceasefire in October 1994 to get their political spokesmen involved in peace talks.

It issued a statement in Belfast saying the new IRA truce was a tactic to get Sinn Fein invited to the multi-party talks, which resume in earnest on September 15 after stumbling to a halt earlier in the year amid an upsurge of sectarian and guerrilla violence
The Lisbellaw bomb was the first since the IRA's truce was declared on July 20, followed by a British move to reduce army patrols protecting police across the province.
But British troops have not been completely withdrawn and Northern Ireland's Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) police are still fully armed and wear flak jackets.
The sight of British armoured personnel carriers sprouting fully armed soldiers with the latest assault rifles is still commonplace on Belfast's busiest shopping streets.

Britain pulled its 18,000-strong army back from the front line of a 28-year conflict and into barracks after an earlier IRA truce in September 1994, but has been on alert since the guerrillas ended that ceasefire in February last year with a string of bomb attacks on the British mainland.
